Entropy measures expected self-information; cross-entropy evaluates a proposed distribution on target outcomes; KL divergence compares the two.
Their shared probability notation also explains classification losses, probability maps, and a Gaussian latent-distribution penalty.
Read [probability](probability.qmd) for random variables and distributions, and [expectations](expectations.qmd) for the averages used below.

## Entropy and self-information {#entropy}

Let $p(x)$ be the probability mass function of a discrete random variable $X$.
Use natural logarithms, so information is measured in nats.
For a discrete outcome with positive probability, its self-information is $-\ln p(x)$.
Entropy is the expected self-information under the same distribution:

$$
  H(p)=-\sum_xp(x)\ln p(x).
$$

The convention $0\ln0=0$ uses a limit.
For continuous densities, the analogous differential entropy can be negative and depends on the coordinate system.

## Cross-entropy {#cross-entropy}

For a discrete target distribution $p$ and predicted distribution $q$, cross-entropy is

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  H(p,q)&=-\sum_xp(x)\ln q(x)\\
  &=-\mathbb E_p[\ln q(X)].
  \end{aligned}
$$

Natural logarithms measure the result in nats.
The negative sign belongs in both expressions.
If $p(x)>0$ but $q(x)=0$, the loss is infinite; zero target masses contribute zero by convention.
Cross-entropy is not a distance: even $H(p,p)$ is generally positive because it equals the target's [entropy](entropy.qmd#entropy).
[KL divergence](entropy.qmd#kl-divergence) measures its excess over that entropy.

## KL divergence {#kl-divergence}

Let $p$ and $q$ be probability mass functions on the same discrete outcome space, and use natural logarithms.
KL divergence measures the excess cross-entropy over the entropy of the source distribution:

$$
  D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)
  =\sum_xp(x)\ln\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.
$$

For finite quantities,

$$
  H(p,q)=H(p)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q).
$$

The convention $0\ln0=0$ uses a limit.
If $p(x)>0$ but $q(x)=0$, the corresponding cross-entropy and KL divergence are infinite.
KL is nonnegative and asymmetric; it does not satisfy all the properties of a metric.
For continuous densities, KL uses an integral.
The terms $H(p)$ and $H(p,q)$ are the entropy and cross-entropy defined above.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: the entropy identity and nonnegative KL"}

Subtract the entropy from the cross-entropy:

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  H(p,q)-H(p)
  &=\sum_xp(x)\bigl(\ln p(x)-\ln q(x)\bigr)\\
  &=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q).
  \end{aligned}
$$

Assume $q>0$ wherever $p>0$.
Since $-\ln$ is convex, [Jensen's inequality](expectations.qmd#jensen) gives

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)
  &=\mathbb E_p\!\left[-\ln\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}\right]\\
  &\geq-\ln\!\left(\sum_{x:p(x)>0}q(x)\right)\\
  &\geq0.
  \end{aligned}
$$

Equality requires $p=q$ as distributions.
This derivation concerns finite discrete distributions; analogous continuous statements require the relevant measures and integrability conditions.

:::

## Binary logits and sigmoid {#sigmoid}

For classification, switch notation: $y$ denotes a target label, while $p$ denotes a predicted class probability rather than the source distribution used above.

A binary classifier can produce an unrestricted real-valued score $z$, called a logit, and convert it into a probability:

$$
  z\;\longrightarrow\;p.
$$

The sigmoid function maps a real score $z$ to a number between zero and one:

$$
  p=\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-z)}.
$$

Here, $\exp$ is the exponential function.
Increasing $z$ increases $p$; at $z=0$, $p=0.5$.
We interpret $p$ as the predicted probability of class $1$.

## The sigmoid derivative {#sigmoid-derivative}

The derivative is

$$
  \sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z)).
$$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: differentiating sigmoid"}

With $p=\sigma(z)$,

$$
  \frac{dp}{dz}
  =\frac{\exp(-z)}{(1+\exp(-z))^2}
  =p(1-p).
$$

:::

## Binary cross-entropy {#binary-cross-entropy}

Let $y\in\{0,1\}$ be the observed target and $p\in(0,1)$ be the predicted probability of class $1$.
The predicted probability of class $0$ is then $1-p$.
Binary cross-entropy for one example is

$$
  \ell(p,y)=-\left[y\ln p+(1-y)\ln(1-p)\right],
$$

where $\ln$ is the natural logarithm.
Because $y$ is either zero or one, it selects one term:

$$
  \ell(p,y)=
  \begin{cases}
    -\ln p,&y=1,\\
    -\ln(1-p),&y=0.
  \end{cases}
$$

In words, take the probability assigned to the observed class, then apply the negative logarithm.
A higher probability for that class produces a lower loss.

## The binary-logit gradient {#binary-logit-gradient}

With the sigmoid probability $p=\sigma(z)$ and fixed target $y$, the loss is now a function of the logit $z$.
For binary cross-entropy composed with sigmoid, the derivative with respect to this score is

$$
  \frac{d\ell}{dz}=p-y.
$$

This is the derivative with respect to $z$.
A parameter derivative also includes how the score depends on that parameter.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: the sigmoid and cross-entropy gradient"}

Holding the target $y$ fixed, differentiate binary cross-entropy with respect to $p$:

$$
  \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial p}
  =-\frac{y}{p}+\frac{1-y}{1-p}
  =\frac{p-y}{p(1-p)}.
$$

The [sigmoid derivative](entropy.qmd#sigmoid-derivative) is $dp/dz=p(1-p)$.

Applying the chain rule, the factors cancel:

$$
  \frac{d\ell}{dz}
  =\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial p}\frac{dp}{dz}
  =\frac{p-y}{p(1-p)}\,p(1-p)
  =p-y.
$$

:::

## Class logits and softmax {#softmax}

For $K\geq2$ classes, softmax converts $K$ real logits into positive probabilities summing to one.

A model can produce one unrestricted real score, or logit, for each class:

$$
  \mathbf z=(z_{\text{cat}},z_{\text{dog}},z_{\text{bird}}).
$$

These scores can be negative, exceed one, and need not sum to one.
Softmax maps a vector of real scores to a probability vector:

$$
  p_k=\frac{\exp(z_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)}.
$$

Here, $k$ identifies the class whose probability we are calculating, while $j$ runs over all classes in the denominator.
Exponentiating each score produces positive weights while preserving their ordering.
Dividing each weight by their sum makes the resulting probabilities sum to one.

## Categorical and soft-target cross-entropy {#categorical-cross-entropy}

For $K\geq2$ classes, let $\mathbf p=(p_1,\ldots,p_K)$ be predicted probabilities satisfying $p_k>0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_k=1$.
Let $\mathbf y=(y_1,\ldots,y_K)$ be a one-hot target: the observed class has entry $1$, and every other entry is $0$.
Categorical cross-entropy for one example is

$$
  \ell(\mathbf p,\mathbf y)=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}y_k\ln p_k.
$$

The index $k$ runs over classes within one example.
Because only the observed class has $y_k=1$, the formula reduces to

$$
  \ell=-\ln p_{\text{observed class}}.
$$

Softmax supplies these probabilities from the class scores.

The target can also be a soft probability vector, with nonnegative entries summing to one, rather than a one-hot label.
The same cross-entropy formula then averages negative log-probabilities over that target distribution.
[Knowledge distillation](../../literature-review/theory/knowledge-distillation.qmd) uses a teacher's softened probabilities and derives the temperature-dependent gradient.

## Discrete targets and continuous probability vectors {#discrete-targets}

The type of a probability vector differs from the type of the random variable it describes.
For a vocabulary of $K$ token IDs, the next token takes one value in $\{1,\ldots,K\}$, while the model assigns $K$ real-valued probabilities that sum to one.
The real-valued entries do not make the token itself a continuous variable.
Cross-entropy evaluates the probability assigned to the observed token.

For example, a distribution assigning probabilities $(0.2,0.7,0.1)$ to three token IDs gives loss $-\ln(0.7)$ when the target is ID $2$.
The numerical ordering of token IDs does not encode distance between their meanings.
Predicting the number $2$ with squared error would impose a different task and geometry.

For an autoregressive sequence, each position predicts a categorical distribution conditioned on the observation and preceding tokens.
Training sums or averages the negative log-probabilities of the observed tokens.
During ordinary generation, the model selects or samples one token and conditions the next prediction on that choice.
The Transformer architecture alone does not require this generation order.

[FAST](../../literature-review/action/fast.qmd) converts continuous action chunks into discrete token sequences for this kind of objective.
[Diffusion Policy](../../literature-review/action/diffusion-policy.qmd) instead predicts continuous noise, and [flow matching](../machine-learning/flow-matching.qmd#flow-matching) predicts a continuous velocity.
Their squared-error targets are different objects from the categorical target in cross-entropy.

## Zero-one loss and accuracy {#zero-one-loss}

Zero-one loss evaluates the predicted class itself.
For a predicted class $\hat c$ and observed class $c$, it assigns

$$
  \ell_{0\text{–}1}(\hat c,c)=
  \begin{cases}
    0,&\hat c=c,\\
    1,&\hat c\ne c.
  \end{cases}
$$

Its average is the fraction of incorrect predictions, so accuracy is one minus that average.
Zero-one loss is constant within regions where the predicted class stays the same.
Small parameter changes within such a region leave its value unchanged, so its ordinary gradient there provides no direction for improvement.
Cross-entropy can decrease as the probability assigned to the observed class increases, even before the predicted class changes.

## KL for a diagonal Gaussian {#gaussian-kl}

Let $q=\mathcal N(\mu,\operatorname{diag}(\sigma^2))$ with all $\sigma_j>0$, and let $p=\mathcal N(0,I)$.
Write $K=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)$.
For $d$ latent coordinates, write the encoder covariance as $\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\ldots,\sigma_d^2)$.
Against a standard Gaussian prior, the KL term has a closed form:

$$
  K=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^{d}
  \left(\mu_j^2+\sigma_j^2-1-\log\sigma_j^2\right).
$$

Each coordinate contributes zero when its mean is zero and its variance is one.
For example, $q=\mathcal N(2,1)$ gives $K=2$ nats, while $q=\mathcal N(0,1)$ gives $K=0$.
The penalty concerns an entire distribution, so zero KL does not mean that its samples all equal the prior mean. [VAE, Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=10).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: the diagonal Gaussian KL"}

Start with $K=\mathbb E_q[\log q(z)-\log p(z)]$.
For independent coordinates, the normalisation constants cancel and leave

$$
  K=\frac12\sum_j\mathbb E_q\left[
  z_j^2-\frac{(z_j-\mu_j)^2}{\sigma_j^2}
  -\log\sigma_j^2\right].
$$

Use $\mathbb E_q[z_j^2]=\mu_j^2+\sigma_j^2$ and $\mathbb E_q[(z_j-\mu_j)^2]=\sigma_j^2$ to obtain the visible formula.
The KL in the ELBO is measured in nats because these logarithms are natural logarithms.

:::

Matching the standard Gaussian prior encourages means and variances toward zero and one, respectively.
It does not force every sampled latent to be zero or guarantee named physical meanings for its coordinates.

## Connections {#connections}

[Likelihood and estimation](likelihood-and-estimation.qmd#classification) derives why classification likelihood gives a mean cross-entropy objective.
[Loss](../machine-learning/loss.qmd#loss-and-risk) distinguishes an individual penalty from its dataset average, and [gradient descent](optimization.qmd#gradient-descent) explains why derivatives matter during optimisation.
[The ELBO](elbo.qmd) uses a KL to the prior in its objective and a different KL to the posterior in its gap.
[Reparameterisation](reparameterization.qmd) distinguishes the Gaussian variance from the standard deviation used when sampling.
